analysis.one_liner: Makes drink and packaging companies pay to collect and recycle single-use plastics and creates a national bottle deposit.
analysis.headline: A plastic pollution bill with 89 Democratic cosponsors was referred to four House committees and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make the companies that make and sell packaged goods pay for the collection, recycling, and disposal of their packaging instead of leaving those costs with cities and taxpayers. It would create a national deposit-refund program for beverage containers starting at 10 cents, require a rising share of recycled plastic in bottles, ban certain plastics like polystyrene and PVC packaging, restrict toxic chemicals such as PFAS and bisphenols in food-contact plastics, set targets to shrink single-use plastic use by 25% by 2032 and 50% by 2050, and limit plastic pellet discharge into waterways. Companies would organize into industry-run nonprofit "Producer Responsibility Organizations" whose plans the EPA would approve, audit, and enforce.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary consumers, who get their deposit back on empty containers; communities near plastics plants and landfills, which get environmental-justice protections and funding; local governments, whose waste and litter cleanup costs shift to producers; and the recycling and composting industries, which receive guaranteed funding streams.

how_it_helps.text: Producers must join Producer Responsibility Organizations that pay the full cost of collecting, sorting, and recycling their packaging, with fees that charge more for hard-to-recycle designs.
A national beverage container deposit of at least 10 cents applies to drink containers up to 3 liters, redeemable at retailers or staffed redemption centers open at least 10 hours a day.
Single-use plastic producers must cut the amount of plastic they put on the market by 25% by 2032, 40% by 2040, and 50% by 2050, shifting to reuse and refill systems.
Plastic beverage bottles must contain at least 15% recycled material by 2025, rising to 60% by 2040, sourced from the United States.

The bill bans packaging made with polystyrene, PVC, carbon-black pigment, and oxodegradable additives, bars toxic substances like PFAS, phthalates, and bisphenols from covered products, and limits plastic pellet discharges from production facilities.
Facilities covered by the bill face environmental-justice requirements designed to prevent low-income communities and communities of color from bearing a disproportionate share of plastic pollution.

analysis.who_pays: Beverage companies, packaged-goods brands, plastics manufacturers, and retailers, who fund the deposit system, recycling fees, and design changes. Those costs would largely be passed into shelf prices, so consumers pay more per item while getting deposits back on containers they return.

drawbacks.text: Producer fees and deposit-program costs would likely be built into retail prices, raising everyday shopping costs; the bill forbids charging the fee as a separate line on a receipt, so consumers would not see it itemized.

The bill waives antitrust law for producers carrying out an approved plan, allowing competing brands in a category to coordinate pricing and infrastructure decisions within their Producer Responsibility Organization.

The recycling-rate and source-reduction mandates phase in slowly, with the first 25% plastic-reduction target not due until 2032, and producers with under $1 million in annual revenue are exempt entirely.

Retailers must accept returned containers and pay refunds during business hours, up to 250 containers per customer per day at large stores, creating handling burdens the bill offsets only through redemption centers and per-customer limits.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would shift billions in waste-management and litter costs from taxpayers to the packaging economy and directly cut a pollutant that shows up in water, food, and human bodies. The honest costs are real: higher prices as fees pass through, a new return-and-refund routine for shoppers, and an antitrust carve-out that lets industry coordinate. The slow phase-ins blunt both the benefit and the near-term cost. On balance it is a well-developed attempt to make packaging producers internalize their own waste, not a badly designed bill.

outcome.mechanism: It sat with four House committees from October 2023 until the Congress ended in January 2025; none of them held a markup or sent it to the floor.

narrative.text: Rep. Jared Huffman introduced the bill on October 25, 2023, with 45 original cosponsors, all Democrats.
It grew to 89 cosponsors, every one a House Democrat, and none a Republican.
The House referred it to the Energy and Commerce, Transportation and Infrastructure, Foreign Affairs, and Agriculture Committees, and it went to subcommittees in each of the first three.
The action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action for the remaining 14 months of the Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Plastic and packaging manufacturers, beverage brands, and retailers avoided new deposit, recycling, and design mandates. Cities and residents continue to pay for collecting and disposing of the waste.

for.name: Rep. Jared Huffman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled 45 original Democratic cosponsors.

for.name: 89 of 216 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no House Republican did.

against.name: Rep. Cathy McMorris Rodgers
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Her committee, the primary referral, took no action on the bill — no hearing, no markup — in the 14 months after referral.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to four committees and never brought it to the floor; no chamber vote ever occurred.

sides.party_line_note: All 89 cosponsors were Democrats and none were Republicans; with Republicans holding the House majority and chairing every committee of referral, no stage of the process ever began.

industries.note: Source-reduction targets, bans on polystyrene and PVC packaging, recycled-content minimums, and pellet discharge limits would cut output and force redesigns. The industry's interest in continuing current production runs against the public's interest in less plastic pollution.

A national 10-cent deposit, rising recycled-content mandates, and responsibility fees would raise costs across every bottled and canned drink sold in America. Unredeemed deposits must be invested in collection and recycling infrastructure.

Brands pay producer fees scaled to how recyclable their packaging is, and retailers must accept container returns, but the fees reward easier-to-recycle designs and the deposit money flows back to consumers who return containers.

Producer-funded plans must pay recyclers and composters and build collection infrastructure, creating a large guaranteed funding stream. Its growth serves the public goal of keeping packaging out of waterways.
